about: MUTATING — writes a partition table and a filesystem, which is the most destructive thing any verb here does. In the shape of design 17835005 (decided by David 2026-09-21 — a rendered plan, signed with his passkey, single-use, verified before the argv is built), and authorised per run by that passkey. It declares requires_approval and names plan-a-disk-commission as its plan_verb, so the runner renders the plan (from the same device_by_id and mount_path) onto the request's approve step, runs this only after a passkey signs it (a presence stamp bound to the plan bytes, under ten minutes old, single-use), and hands the script sha256 of the SIGNED plan as plan_sha256 (backlog fd7090cc). It was INERT until its script took that hash (backlog b2d5b546, 2026-09-26): the runner refuses an approval verb that cannot re-render its plan and refuse one that drifted since it was signed (q4: drift voids an approval). Its bound is by construction of the ONE script it calls (infra/forge/commission-a-disk.sh), tightened by the adversarial review of its car (2026-09-27): the target must be a /dev/disk/by-id/ name that does not end in -partN, resolving to a device lsblk types as a whole disk (not a partition, dm, md or loop node), with no partitions, no signature wipefs can find (filesystem, LUKS, LVM, RAID or ZFS member, partition table), nothing mounted, and not in the chain backing /; the mount path must be one new directory under /srv, empty or absent, not a symlink, not mounted on and not already an fstab target, and /etc/fstab must verify as it stands; all re-checked immediately before the write rather than once at plan time, each fact failing closed. The write re-renders the plan with the command --plan uses and refuses (exit 78, nothing written) unless its bytes still hash to the approved plan_sha256; the plan carries every observed fact and the act itself (the parted, mkfs and mount argv and the fstab line, from the arrays the write runs). The fstab entry is by UUID with nofail and a 10 s device timeout, written to a copy that findmnt verifies before it is renamed over /etc/fstab, and only that one mount is mounted; any failure after the first write is exit 1, naming the state it left. A kernel name is refused outright — on 2026-09-21 adding a disk to the forge renumbered the devices and the drive that looked like the new one by number was the one carrying the system.
